opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest legacy is showing that reinforcement learning combined with planning and search really works at scale. AlphaGo was the first time we had a system that went beyond imitating human data and discovered new knowledge. Move 37 is the famous example: a move no human expert would have played, which turned out to be brilliant. That showed us an agent can learn from its own experience and surpass the data it started with.

AlphaZero took that further by removing the human data entirely. Starting from random play and learning purely through self-play, it reached superhuman level in Go, chess, and shogi with one algorithm. The lesson there was generality: if you have the right learning signal and enough compute, you don't need to hand-engineer domain knowledge.

MuZero removed another assumption, which was that you need a perfect simulator of the environment. It learned its own model of the world, but only the parts that matter for planning: value, policy, and reward. That's important for agents, because in the real world you never get the rules handed to you.

When I look at agents today, especially those built on large language models, I see these ideas returning. Pretraining gives you a strong prior, much like AlphaGo's supervised initialization. The frontier now is applying RL on top of that: letting models try things, get feedback, and improve, whether through verifiable rewards in math and code or through longer-horizon tasks. Test-time compute, where models think longer and explore different reasoning paths before answering, is spiritually very close to search in AlphaZero. You trade inference compute for better decisions.

The open question, and the hard part, is that games gave us a clean reward signal and a perfect simulator. The real world gives you neither. So much of the work now is figuring out how to get reliable feedback, how to build good environments, and how to make planning work when the world is messy and open-ended. But the core recipe of a strong prior, learning from experience, and spending compute on search and reasoning is, I think, the lasting contribution of that line of work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important legacy is actually a fairly simple idea: that you can get superhuman performance by combining learning with search, and that the learning can come from the system's own experience rather than from humans.

With AlphaGo, we started with human games. We trained a policy network to imitate strong players, then improved it with self-play, and we combined that with Monte Carlo tree search. The lesson there was that neural networks could give you intuition, a sense of which moves are worth looking at and how good a position is, and search could sharpen that intuition into something precise. Neither on its own was enough. Pure search had plateaued for years in Go, and pure pattern matching makes mistakes a strong player would exploit.

AlphaZero took away the human data entirely. That was the moment, for me, where it became clear that the bottleneck wasn't the data we had, it was the quality of the learning loop. The system played itself, used search to generate better moves than the raw network would produce, and then trained the network to match the search. Search became a kind of teacher. You can think of it as a policy improvement operator. The network proposes, search refines, the network learns from the refinement, and you iterate. The same algorithm worked for Go, chess, and shogi without any game-specific knowledge beyond the rules.

MuZero removed one more assumption, which is that you need to know the rules. It learned a model of the environment, but not a model that tried to predict pixels or reconstruct the board. It learned only what mattered for planning: the value, the policy, and the reward. That's a subtle but important point. A good model for decision making doesn't have to be a faithful simulator of the world. It has to be useful for the decisions you care about.

So when I think about what this means for building agents today, a few things stand out.

First, the idea of using compute at inference time to improve on what the model would do by default. That's exactly what we're seeing now with reasoning models. Thinking longer, sampling multiple candidates, verifying, searching over chains of reasoning. These are all forms of search on top of a learned prior. The pretrained model is the intuition, and the extra compute is the deliberation.

Second, the idea that the output of that deliberation can become training data. If your agent reasons for a long time and arrives at a better answer, you can train the base model on that better answer, and now the fast path improves. That's the AlphaZero loop, applied to language and to tasks that aren't games.

Third, and this is where it gets harder, the games had a few things that made this very clean. The environment was perfectly simulated, so self-play was free. The reward was unambiguous. You won or you lost. And the state was fully observed. Most of the agent problems we care about today don't have any of those properties. The real world is expensive to interact with, rewards are sparse or subjective, and the agent sees only a fraction of what's going on. So the legacy isn't a recipe you can copy directly. It's a set of principles that you have to adapt.

The question I find myself asking is: where is the verifier? In Go, the game itself was the verifier. For code, you have tests. For math, you can check proofs. For a lot of open-ended tasks, you don't have anything like that, and you end up relying on learned reward models, which brings you back to human judgment with all its limitations. Figuring out how to get strong learning signals in domains without a clean referee is, to me, the central unsolved problem, and it's where the lessons from those systems point without quite telling you the answer.

astra-6.text:
I think the central legacy is that learning and planning can reinforce each other. An agent can learn from experience, use what it has learned to make better decisions, and then generate better experience through those decisions.

AlphaGo showed how powerful that combination could be. AlphaZero pushed it further by learning through self-play, with less dependence on human examples. MuZero took another step: the agent could learn a model useful for planning without being given the environment’s rules.

For agents today, I think the interesting question is how to make that loop work beyond games. In a game, the objective is clear, and you can generate experience and evaluate progress very precisely. In the real world, objectives are less clear, feedback can be delayed, and mistakes can be costly. So these systems give us a powerful foundation, but making agents that learn and plan reliably in open-ended environments remains a substantial challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central lesson is that learning and planning work very well together. You don’t have to choose between a system that learns from experience and a system that searches for what to do next. Learning can make search more useful, and search can produce better experience to learn from.

There’s a progression across those systems. AlphaGo combined learning from human games with self-play and search. AlphaZero showed how much could emerge from self-play without human examples, given the rules of the game. MuZero took another step: it learned a model that was useful for planning without being given the environment’s dynamics. That model didn’t need to reconstruct every detail of the world; it needed to capture what mattered for choosing actions.

For agents today, that raises a very interesting question: what should an agent learn about its environment so that it can reason about the consequences of its actions? Games give you clear objectives and relatively cheap experience. The real world is much less forgiving. So I see these systems as demonstrating powerful principles, while leaving us with the challenge of making those principles work when feedback is ambiguous, experience is expensive, and the task isn’t neatly specified.
